data.title: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska
data.description:
Kreiss-Tomkins becomes first Democrat since 1998 elected governor in Alaska

BECKY BOHRER
Updated Sat, November 14, 2026 at 5:07 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Election 2026 Alaska Governor

1 of 2
FILE - Alaska gubernatorial candidate Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, speaks to people outside a convention center in Juneau, Alaska, June 6, 2026. (AP Photo/Becky Bohrer, File) (AP Photo/Becky Bohrer)

JUNEAU, Alaska (AP) — Alaska voters have elected a Democrat for governor for the first time since 1998, part of a national midterm elections wave that gave the party sweeping wins in state governments across the country.

Former state lawmaker Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins defeated three Republicans, including one endorsed by President Donald Trump. His victory means Democrats will control the governor's office in 30 states, including several they flipped after years of Republican control in places such as Iowa, Georgia, Ohio and Texas.

Kreiss-Tomkins, often referred to as JKT, completed a political comeback three years after leaving the state House. He traveled throughout Alaska to build his coalition and focused on affordability, advocated for full funding of public schools and called for all oil and gas producers to pay corporate income tax. He also sought a moratorium on new data centers until state lawmakers pass regulations for their development.

Advertisement

He said Alaska had become "broken" under eight years of outgoing Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy and needed a change. He cited among other issues a state ferry system that he said has been left in shambles, with routes to many communities cut drastically. The ferry is a key mode of transportation for southeast Alaska communities not connected by roads, some of which also have limited air service.

Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, emphasized a willingness to work across party lines and said he wanted a Cabinet with Republicans, Democrats and independents.

"If they're competent, if they're service-minded, if they're entrepreneurial, if they're problem-solvers, you're on the team. Game on," he said during a candidate forum last month. "Let's go, and let's get Alaska back on track."

Republican U.S. Sen. Lisa Murkowski, who has at times been at odds with her party, including Trump, endorsed Kreiss-Tomkins a week before the election. She said Kreiss-Tomkins "understands that governing requires listening to people with different perspectives and finding common ground to solve the problems all of us face."

Three former governors including Democrat Tony Knowles, independent Bill Walker and Republican Frank Murkowski, the senator's father, also endorsed him.

In a statement declaring victory earlier Friday, Kreiss-Tomkins said voters wanted change and "a government that works across party lines to move Alaska forward. Our administration will not waste a single day getting to work to solve problems for Alaska." He said his campaign had more than 10,000 donors.

His campaign did not immediately respond to requests for comment after The Associated Press called the race.

He defeated Republicans Bernadette Wilson, Dave Bronson and Treg Taylor. Trump had endorsed Wilson, a business owner, and criticized the other Republican candidates for staying in the race. Bronson is a former mayor of Anchorage, Alaska's largest city, while Taylor was a state attorney general under Dunleavy.

Bronson congratulated Kreiss-Tomkins on social media and wished him success. A message seeking comment from Wilson's campaign was not immediately returned.

Many Republicans saw ranking as their party's best shot of retaining the governor's seat. It was a message that conflicted with that of Trump, who has consistently complained about Alaska's unusual voting method, including during a rally in Alaska in October.

Kreiss-Tomkins finished first in August's open primary, followed by a second Democrat, Tom Begich, who withdrew from the race. Begich's campaign at the time said it had concluded that the "strongest path to victory is to bring Democratic voters, donors and resources together behind one candidate." Wilson finished third in the primary.

Kreiss-Tomkins said compromise "is a virtue, not a dirty word," and said he saw the mission of the new governor as working with lawmakers to resolve longstanding problems in the state.

The state's last Democratic governor, Tony Knowles, left office in 2002 after serving back-to-back terms. Walker served from 2014 to 2018.

Kreiss-Tomkins will be sworn in Dec. 7. His lieutenant governor is Zac Johnson, an independent.

data.title: After 26 years, the U.S. has lost its measles elimination status
data.description:
Nearly all measles cases have been in people who had not received the highly effective measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

Thanks to widespread vaccination, measles had been considered “eliminated” as a continually transmitting illness in the United States since 2000 – but not anymore.

An independent commission of experts that reports to the director of the Pan American Health Organization determined that the US no longer qualified as having eliminated measles, a source close to the process told CNN on Friday.

The news was first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

The decision was widely expected after years of falling vaccination levels and surging case counts, but it’s still a black mark on the nation’s public health policy.

The international committee that determines countries’ measles elimination status considers an infection to be endemic, or regularly occurring, if infections caused by the same strain are passed from person to person for at least a year within the same country.

To determine this, the committee members look at the genetic code of viruses sampled from patients.

Related article

The US has had the tools to control measles for almost 65 years. Here’s how it’s come raging back

6 min read

Every time a virus copies itself, it makes tiny changes in its genetic code. By studying the genomes of different viruses in an outbreak, scientists can determine how closely the infections may be related and whether they are likely to have been part of the same chains of transmission.

In August, scientists with Utah’s public health laboratory published a preprint study showing that the same strain of measles had been circulating in the state for more than a year, accounting for more than 95% of cases there. It traveled from the southwest part of the state to central Utah, ultimately causing more than 600 cases between June 2025 and June 2026.

There have also been sustained outbreaks in South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin and New York, as well as other states.

It’s not clear what data the committee relied on to make its decision, but it wasn’t exactly a tough call, said Dr. Angela Rassmussen, a virologist at the University of Saskatchewan in Canada and Editor-in-Chief of the journal Vaccine. The Utah data alone would have been enough to make the case, she said.

The US has logged record numbers of measles cases, hospitalizations and deaths for the past two years, even as some members of the Trump administration – including President Donald Trump – have cast doubt on the safety and effectiveness of the vaccines that prevent it.

“Measles elimination is a vital sign for our public health system. It shows cracks in our foundation. Losing elimination status means that we are less prepared as a nation to address infectious and noninfectious disease challenges,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, former director of the National Center for Immunization and Respiratory Diseases at the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Related article
Erica Schwartz testifies during a Senate Health Education Labor and Pensions committee confirmation hearing, to be the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, on July 15.

CDC chief says agency will not change measles response if US loses elimination status

3 min read

The measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) vaccine is so effective that two doses cut an exposed person’s chances of getting sick by 97% compared with someone who is unvaccinated.

Since 2000, when measles was declared eliminated in the United States, the country has still some outbreaks every year. These were touched off by sick travelers who brought the virus into the country. Because of community protection maintained by high vaccination rates, these outbreaks were usually small and short-lived.

In 2025 and 2026, however, the virus found more families and communities that were unvaccinated, leaving them vulnerable to infection.

More than 5,400 measles cases have been reported in the US this year – the highest number since 1991. Most are linked to the 43 new outbreaks this year, but more than 1,000 cases are linked to outbreaks that began last year.

Nearly all of this year’s cases have been in people who had not received the MMR vaccine or whose vaccination status is unknown. People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported cases, according to the CDC, and at least 10 people have died after catching measles, according to state reports.

‘Measles is back’

The declaration is a humbling moment for a nation that played a leading role in ridding the world of smallpox – the only human disease to have ever been wiped out worldwide – and worked for decades to drive measles offshore.

“This is just so devastating and so sad that we are where we are today,” said Dr. Nuwan Gunawardhana, an infectious disease epidemiologist at Columbia University Irvine Medical Center in New York. “This just kind of points towards the direction of really reversing a generation of public health progress.”

But it also means people who are too young to be vaccinated against measles or who have lowered immune function because of organ transplants or cancer or other conditions are at higher risk in areas with outbreaks than they were just two years ago.

People have been hospitalized in roughly 1 in 9 reported measles cases this year, according to the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

Most people who get measles will recover after having a fever and a rash and feeling generally miserable for several days, said Dr. William Moss, a professor and measles expert at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. But that doesn’t mean the infection is benign, he said.

Measles can also wipe out a person’s immune memory. The immune system forgets which infections it’s fought off before, leaving the person vulnerable to secondary threats like pneumonia or diarrhea.

If a pregnant woman catches measles, she can pass it to her baby in the womb, and the baby will be born with measles, putting its life at risk.

In rare cases, people who’ve had measles can develop serious neurologic complications, sometimes years after the original infection. The most serious is subacute sclerosing panencephalitis, or SSPE, which is progressive and fatal.

All of these complications can be prevented by vaccination.

The United States losing its measles elimination status is “incredibly embarrassing,” said Dr. Peter Hotez, co-director of the Center for Vaccine Development at Texas Children’s Hospital in Houston. But, he said, it’s a signal of an more important message: “Basically, measles is back.”

“Whether or not we’ve officially lost our elimination status to me is much less important than, basically, measles is here. It’s pervasive, and vaccination rates are down across the country, and I don’t see us getting back to normal anytime soon,” he added.

Could the US regain its elimination status?

Measles is one of the most contagious viruses known to science. A single infected person typically spreads it to 12 to 18 others. The virus is airborne and can float in a room for hours after a sick person leaves it.

Soon after the measles vaccine was deployed in the early 1960s, public health experts realized that if enough people in an area were vaccinated, the protection from the shot could stop the spread of the virus. The US set its first goal to eliminate measles transmission in 1978.

Measles is one of the 30 diseases targeted for elimination by 2030 by the Pan American Health Organization, or PAHO.

In 2016, PAHO and the World Health Organization declared the 35 countries in the Americas region to be free of ongoing measles transmission.

That designation was lost last year, however, when Canada elimination status ended after a lengthy outbreak that spanned several provinces.

Related article

Tracking measles cases in the United States

3 min read

Mexico, which has had several large measles outbreaks of its own, is also in danger of losing its elimination status.

Moss said that since the US has lost its measles elimination status, it has to be on the path to regaining it.

“That’s not easy, particularly in the current environment with diminished public trust in vaccines, the increasing nonmedical exemptions that we’re seeing in schools, and declines in measles, mumps and rubella vaccination among our kindergarten students, and the undermining of vaccine policy,” Moss said.

“So it’s not going to be a trivial task for the United States to regain its measles elimination status.”

data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin plan unprecedented summit as wars strain global relations
data.description:
Trump, Xi and Putin plan an unprecedented joint meeting on the sidelines of APEC, White House says

AAMER MADHANI, HUIZHONG WU and VLADIMIR ISACHENKOV
Updated Fri, November 13, 2026 at 11:40 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The leaders of the United States, China and Russia plan to meet Thursday on the sidelines of next week's Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China's tech hub of Shenzhen — an unprecedented gathering of the heads of the world's biggest nuclear powers.

While the leaders gathering for joint talks will mark a singular moment, analysts say expectations are low that the talks will lead to major breakthroughs and say they will be heavier in symbolism than substance.

Plans for the three-way summit with Donald Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin were confirmed Friday by the White House. It comes at a complicated moment in relations between the three countries.

Advertisement

Trump has warmly embraced Xi after coming to a truce in their short-lived trade war last year and in spite of differences over the U.S. war with Iran and other tensions between the world's foremost economic powers.

Similarly, Trump has sought to build his relationship with Putin, even as the Russian leader has persisted in his nearly 5-year-old war with Ukraine and as Moscow has deepened its military, intelligence and diplomatic partnership with Iran.

The U.S. president has insisted that such a meeting would provide an opportunity for the three leaders to discuss the U.S. war with Iran and his goal of reaching a three-way agreement on their nuclear arms stockpiles.

Trump does plan on discussing the Iran war with Xi and Putin, but will steer away from discussing Ukraine, according to a senior U.S. official who briefed reporters on the condition of anonymity.

The last nuclear arms pact between Russia and the United States expired in February, removing caps on the two largest atomic arsenals for the first time in more than a half-century. When that treaty — known as New START — expired, Trump rejected a call by Russia to extend the two-country deal for another year and called for "a new, improved and modernized" deal that includes China.

The trilateral meeting is intended to serve as the "beginning of hopefully a conversation" on nuclear disarmament "that can be productive going forward," said the U.S. official, who added that no agreements are expected to be announced.

But Beijing's arsenal of more than 600 warheads, according to Pentagon estimates, is far smaller than inventories held by the U.S. and Russia, each estimated to have more than 5,000 warheads. With U.S. and Russian arsenals dwarfing its stockpile, China has shown little interest in developing a nuclear pact.

Trump administration officials acknowledge that the nuclear stockpile issue is a difficult one for Beijing to engage on, but the U.S. official characterized the meeting as the moment for China to "step up ... to the adult table" on a matter of international importance.

Beijing was least certain about the value of the summit

By agreeing to host the meeting, Xi may be calculating that the moment offers him an opportunity to flex China's growing clout and prestige.

For the Kremlin, the planned trilateral meeting is a coveted chance to posture as a superpower on par with Washington and Beijing.

"I think the key for Putin was that this was very much about signaling a desire to talk to the president and talk to Chairman Xi in a way that suggests that they're making decisions on Ukraine, which obviously the Ukrainians and the Europeans don't like," said Edgard Kagan, a former U.S. ambassador to Malaysia who is now at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

The trilateral could very well overshadow the APEC summit. The summit, which is bringing 21 economies to Shenzhen, marks a big moment for China to show off its fast-growing, ultramodern coastal metropolis that transformed from a small fishing village into a global technology and economic hub in just a few decades.

More substantively, such a gathering could also muddy China's argument that a Cold War mentality in the West was a contributing factor that led to Russia's war on Ukraine and its pointed criticism that the U.S. has undermined international institutions and treaties with how it has executed its war against Iran.

The trilateral meeting could undercut China's push to portray itself as a defender of free trade at APEC, said Hoo Tiang Boon, a professor of Chinese foreign policy at Nanyang Technological University.

"You sort of run counter to Chinese support of multilateralism," he said.

The leaders have met in pairs plenty of times over the years

Putin and Xi are no strangers. They've fostered a close personal relationship, meeting more than 40 times since Xi became president in 2013 and addressing each other as "dear friend."

Trump and Putin have met face-to-face on seven different occasions, most recently in Alaska in August 2025. Xi and Trump have held face-to-face talks on eight occasions, including a September state visit to Washington by Xi.

Beijing is the No. 1 trading partner for Moscow, a relationship that has strengthened since Putin sent troops into Ukraine in 2022.

As the EU and the West sought to economically isolate Russia, China increased its purchases of Russia's energy resources and became Moscow's principal supplier of key technologies, including high-tech components for Russian weapons industries. Beijing has ignored Western demands to cut those supplies.

In the lead-up to Russia's war on Ukraine, Xi and Putin declared their countries had a "no-limits friendship." China officially has said it is neutral on the conflict, while charging that Kyiv's Western allies played a part in provoking Russia's military action in Ukraine.

Moscow, in turn, has repeatedly declared its support for Beijing's policy on issues related to Taiwan.

Trump recently struck a diesel deal with Russia, waiving sanctions against Moscow and allowing for the sale of millions of tons of the fuel. The U.S. leader has blamed surging energy prices on Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries. Analysts, however, say the rise in global crude prices is due mostly to the Iran war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has expressed concern that the trilateral meeting could serve as a platform for discussing a possible Ukraine deal behind Kyiv's back.

Planning for the summit has drawn comparisons to the Yalta Conference, the 1945 gathering at which the leaders of the U.S., Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalized plans for establishing the United Nations.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov has dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting that any potential agreements reached in Shenzhen can't be enforced on others.

"It's clear that a meeting between the leaders of countries such as Russia, China and the United States is extremely significant," Peskov said. "However, let's not forget that the vision for a global order is that no one tries to impose any particular view of global order, and it should be based entirely on mutual benefit and mutual respect."

___

Wu reported from Bangkok and Isachenkov from Moscow.

data.title: SpaceX's Starship double catch thwarted as booster ends up in Gulf of Mexico
data.description:
1. Tech
  2. Science

SpaceX’s attempt for a Starship double catch is thwarted when the booster ends up in Gulf of Mexico

Associated Press
MARCIA DUNN
UpdatedFri, November 13, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
Add to Preferred Sources
UpdatedFri, November 13, 2026 at 5:30 PM UTC
1 / 5

SpaceX Starship Launch

SpaceX's mega rocket Starship is stacked and prepared for a test flight from Starbase, Texas, Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026. (AP Photo/Eric Gay)

STARBASE, Texas (AP) — SpaceX launched Starship toward orbit Friday in its boldest test yet: a 22-hour flight that aimed to capture the entire rocket in a move meant to accelerate moon and Mars travel.

But Elon Musk's company had to lower its expectations when the first part of the double catch flopped.

The first-stage booster malfunctioned and instead of returning to its Texas pad several minutes after liftoff, it ended up in the Gulf of Mexico after an automatic abort. Despite the setback, the bullet-shaped spacecraft continued toward orbit. It will steer toward the pad Saturday for a similar grab, barring further trouble.

Advertisement
Advertisement

It's the first time that the spacecraft will try to return to the pad from orbit, to be plucked in midair by mechanical arms secured to the launch tower.

The original goal was to retrieve every single piece of the rocket for the purpose of future recycling, something yet to be achieved anywhere in the world. Musk sees this leading to the kind of fast and consistent launch rates necessary for building moon bases and sending people to Mars.

Once in orbit, Starship will deliver 26 of the company's most advanced Starlink satellites. The plan is for Starship to complete 15 laps around the world at an altitude of around 170 miles (275 kilometers) before heading back to the launch site for Saturday's grand finale.

SpaceX had already made three booster grabs at the company's sprawling Starbase near the U.S.-Mexico border. This was the first attempt to capture the upgraded version that stretches 236 feet (72 meters) — the production model for moon and Mars expeditions. It will also be the first time the company attempts to catch the spacecraft, which spans 171 feet (52 meters). Together, they form the world's biggest and most powerful rocket — an astounding 407 feet (124 meters) in height.

Advertisement
Advertisement

The spacecraft portion of the 14 previous Starships ended up in the ocean, either by design at flight's end or by accident in a stream of flaming wreckage. During the first full-scale test flight in 2023, multiple engines failed to ignite and the tumbling rocket's self-destruct system was activated.

The last test, in September, was the first to reach orbit, but SpaceX did not try to recover any of the rocket stages.

SpaceX plans to start launching Starships from Florida within a few months and from Louisiana in a few years. Scaled-up infrastructure, combined with full rocket reusability, is "how you go from zero launches to 10 to 100 to 1,000 to 10,000 to 100,000," SpaceX's Kiko Dontchev, vice president of launch, said at a NASA tech summit last week at Florida's Kennedy Space Center.

SpaceX's smaller Falcon rockets will continue to fly from Cape Canaveral, carrying astronauts to the International Space Station for NASA and from California carrying Starlinks. Satellites also will keep hitching Falcon rides for now. Musk wants Starships to eventually replace Falcons.

Advertisement
Advertisement

Falcon rockets "are still not fully reusable. We still throw that second stage away every single flight. Starship, we're going to catch both the first stage and second stage," Dontchev said.

NASA is paying SpaceX billions of dollars to land Artemis astronauts on the moon with Starships. Jeff Bezos' Blue Origin is the other major player. NASA expects to decide a year before the Artemis IV lunar landing — the first by astronauts in more than half a century — whether to get the moonwalkers to the surface with Musk's Starship or Bezos' Blue Moon.

During next summer's Artemis III mission, astronauts will practice docking their capsule with a Blue Moon and then a Starship in orbit around Earth. That will set the stage for an Artemis moon touchdown as early as 2028.

data.title: Lauren Boebert loses House seat to Democratic challenger in Colorado
data.description:
Lauren Boebert loses House seat to Democratic challenger in Colorado

The congresswoman had switched districts in the 2024 election to one that favored Republicans, but it wasn't enough to insulate her from widespread Democratic gains this year.

Dylan Stableford, Mike Bebernes
Updated Fri, November 13, 2026 at 8:12 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

In what had been considered Colorado's most Republican-leaning congressional district, incumbent Rep. Lauren Boebert has been defeated by Democrat Eileen Laubacher.

The Associated Press called the race on Friday afternoon.

Laubacher received 48.8% of the vote (187,488 votes) to Boebert's 47.9% (184,047 votes), with 99% of the vote counted. Douglas Mangeris, a libertarian, received 3.3%, or 12,720 votes, per AP. 

Advertisement

Boebert, an outspoken gun rights activist, has served in Congress since 2021 and is considered one of President Trump's staunchest allies on Capitol Hill.

Laubacher is a retired U.S. Navy rear admiral who was deployed in Afghanistan. She also served on the National Security Council under President Joe Biden.

Laubacher's victory adds Colorado's 4th District to the more than 40 Republican-held districts that have flipped to Democrats this midterm cycle, including two others in Colorado. 

In an interview with NewsNation on Thursday, Boebert blamed her impending loss on "so many different variables" that plagued Republicans across the country, including gas prices, the war in Iran and Congress's failure to address corruption in the U.S. political system.

She also argued that she and other members of the right wing House Freedom Caucus "weren't heard" when they called for Congress to take action on a variety of issues that voters care about, including government surveillance and "fair elections."

The result is indicative of the remarkable swing toward Democrats that took place in historically safe Republican districts across the country. Boebert, who relocated from Colorado's more-purple 3rd District in 2023, won by more than 11 percentage points the last time she was on the ballot.

Who is Eileen Laubacher?

Laubacher served 34 years in the U.S. Navy, working in a variety of intelligence and command positions, before retiring in 2024. Her father also spent his career in the Navy, reaching the rank of vice admiral. Her grandfather served as a Navy combat diver during World War II. Laubacher spent significant periods of her Navy career abroad, including a deployment to Afghanistan in 2009 and service in a senior role at the U.S. Embassy in India. 

Though she said she had frequently told people in her life that she would "never run for office," Laubacher opted to enter the race for Boebert's seat because she believed residents of Colorado's 4th District deserved "serious and honest representation" in Congress. 

Laubacher had reportedly been a Republican throughout much of her life before registering as a Democrat in late 2025. Her decision to switch parties, she said, was driven by her view that the Republican Party had become "nearly unrecognizable" to her.

Laubacher's recent party swap became the subject of a lawsuit during the Democratic primary, with one of the other Democrats in the race attempting to prevent her from qualifying for the ballot. That effort failed, and Laubacher later secured the Democratic nomination.

In terms of policy, Laubacher is firmly within the moderate wing of the Democratic Party. She supports strong immigration enforcement, tax cuts for the middle class and reducing the national debt. She placed a heavy emphasis on affordability throughout her campaign, including calling on President Trump to repeal tariffs that raise consumer prices and end the war with Iran. 

Boebert's tenure

First elected to represent Colorado's 3rd District in 2020, Boebert quickly became one of the more vocal and recognizable members of the House Republican caucus. She has been a persistent critic of the "deep state" and was a staunch supporter of Trump's efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election. 

During her first year in the House, she introduced separate resolutions to impeach then-President Joe Biden and Vice President Kamala Harris over their handling of the U.S. military withdrawal from Afghanistan. In 2023, she was one of the key voices behind a leadership battle among House Republicans that was only settled when Kevin McCarthy was elected Speaker after 15 roll call votes. Later that year, she mounted a second unsuccessful effort to impeach Biden. 

Boebert's personal life drew scrutiny in September 2023 after she and a male companion were escorted out of a stage production of Beetlejuice for allegedly "vaping, singing, [and] causing a disturbance." Though she initially denied acting inappropriately, she later apologized for her behavior, saying that her actions "fell short of my values."

Though Boebert won her first House race by a comfortable margin, she narrowly avoided defeat in her bid for reelection in 2022, defeating her Democratic challenger by just 546 votes. Prior to the 2024 election, Boebert switched her reelection bid to Colorado's 4th District, a region of the state considered "far more favorable to Republicans."

The move proved effective in helping Boebert secure a comfortable victory in 2024. But the redder district was not enough to insulate her from the widespread Democratic gains across the country this year.

data.title: Supreme Court will consider Trump order suspending asylum access at the border
data.description:
Supreme Court will consider Trump’s executive order suspending asylum access at the southern border

LINDSAY WHITEHURST
Updated Fri, November 13, 2026 at 6:54 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

WASHINGTON (AP) — The Supreme Court agreed Friday to consider President Donald Trump's ban on asylum at the southern border, a pillar of the Republican president's far-reaching crackdown on immigration.

The Trump administration is asking the justices to overturn lower court decisions that found it was illegal to block asylum applications in an executive order that called the situation at the southern border an "invasion." The suit is the latest in a series of immigration cases before the high court.

Federal law allows people to seek asylum if they fear persecution in their home countries, no matter how they arrived in the U.S.

Advertisement

At the same time, it also allows the executive branch to decide whether people are granted asylum. The Trump administration argues it can categorically deny asylum to migrants covered by the order and should not have to accept applications destined to be rejected.

Federal attorneys say yearslong processing times had previously contributed to a major influx of migrants at the southern border as many were released into the country while awaiting a decision.

But attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union and several immigration rights groups counter that border crossings were already falling before Trump took office.

They say his executive order is an unlawful attempt to unilaterally "eviscerate" legal protections aimed at protecting people fleeing danger in their home countries.

The executive branch does decide whether to grant asylum, which allows people to live and work legally in the U.S. But those decisions are supposed to be made on an individual basis and the law doesn't allow the president to unilaterally stop people from even applying, immigration attorneys argue.

The asylum ban was one of a series of immigration restrictions Trump rolled out upon his return to office in 2025. It has remained in place during the litigation.

The justices are expected to hear the case in the coming months and hand down a decision by the end of June.

It's the third major immigration case the high court will hear this term. The justices will also decide whether people can be swiftly deported to countries other than their homelands and if immigrants can be detained indefinitely during deportation proceedings.

The justices decided another asylum case in favor of the administration earlier this year, clearing the way for the Trump administration to potentially revive a "metering" policy that has been used to turn back immigrants in years past.

data.title: U.S. reportedly offered little help as Singapore probed Nvidia chip shipments
data.description:
Exclusive
World

Singapore held Alice Huang's passport for months, but got little help from U.S. on Nvidia chip probe, sources say

By
Ramy Inocencio
Correspondent
Ramy Inocencio is a CBS News foreign correspondent based in London, covering Europe and the Middle East. He joined the Network in 2019 as CBS News' Asia correspondent, based in Beijing and reporting across the Asia-Pacific, bringing two decades of experience working and traveling between Asia and the United States.
Read Full Bio
Ramy Inocencio

November 13, 2026 / 12:16 PM EST / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Singaporean authorities seized the passport of then-Megaspeed chief executive Alice Huang in June 2025 and held it for eight months, preventing her departure while trying to engage the U.S. government to support their investigation into advanced Nvidia chips possibly being shipped to China.

One source with knowledge of the matter told CBS News on Friday the Singaporean government received no meaningful help from Washington during the time she was in the Asian city-state. This source said officials in Washington were "not forthcoming" in response to Singapore's requests for help, and no substantive assistance has been provided to date.

Singapore's government confirmed in a statement this week that it reached out to both the U.S. Department of Justice and the FBI for assistance with its investigation.

Alice Huang is the suspected Chinese spy at the center of the extramarital affair scandal that toppled Nvidia founder Jensen Huang from the helm of the global tech giant he built over three decades.

Since February 2025, Singaporean authorities have been investigating whether Alice Huang and Megaspeed worked with California-based Supermicro to ship the Silicon Valley firm's computer servers — equipped with advanced Nvidia chips — to China, the source told CBS News. 

Alice Huang flew into Singapore in June 2025 for a voluntary interview with Singapore-based investigators from the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, according to the source. 

The agency sits within the U.S. Department of Commerce and regulates the export of sensitive products on national security and economic grounds. The American authorities requested the interview, according to a Thursday statement by Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry, as part of a post-shipment verification check, a process used to determine whether imported products have reached their declared recipient.

Singaporean police also interviewed Huang on the same day as the U.S. officials, and made the decision to impound her passport. 

The source said it was not known where Huang, a Chinese national, arrived in Singapore from in June 2025. 

By February 2026, however, the Singapore Police Force had not charged Huang with any crime and had no option but to return her passport, the source told CBS News. She was barred from ever returning to Singapore, as authorities assessed that she had given "inaccurate information" to downplay her role at Megaspeed, as noted in the statement from the home ministry.

That statement was released four days after Jensen Huang admitted to having an affair with a woman who sources confirmed to CBS News was Alice Huang. 

Singapore's investigation has focused on whether the then-Megaspeed CEO may have broken domestic law by lying about the details of purchases of computer servers from Supermicro, a San Jose-based technology company. The company's servers use Nvidia's advanced chips to run artificial intelligence software, data centers and cloud computing.

"The suspected domestic offenses pertained to potential false declarations in relation to the purchase of servers and other related offenses," Singapore's Home Affairs Ministry said in its statement this week.  

Singaporean investigators have tried to determine the true ultimate destination of the Supermicro servers ordered by Megaspeed. 

A second source familiar with the investigation told CBS News it is believed they may have been sent to Malaysia, but Singaporean investigators suspect "some or all" of them may then have been shipped onward to China. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing. 

Singapore's home ministry attempted to contact Supermicro, but the U.S. company only "provided limited cooperation," according to the home ministry statement. 

The New York Times reported Wednesday that Malaysia kept Nvidia's chips and installed them in its own data centers, but then rented use of those centers to China, rather than physically shipping any chips to China.

Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said Friday that there was "no indication" any chips linked to the Nvidia-Megaspeed issue had been re-exported out of the country. 

Beijing has dismissed the claims that Alice Huang is a Chinese spy as "groundless speculation" and "nothing more than an attempt to smear China." Asked Thursday about a Bloomberg report that she had returned to China, Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning told reporters: "I do not have information on what you mentioned." 

Since 2022, the U.S. has restricted the export of Nvidia's most powerful chips to China over national security concerns as the world's two biggest economies race for dominance in the AI sector. 

The Singapore police first raised the issue with U.S. authorities in July 2025 to try to secure Supermicro's cooperation in revealing where its servers were ultimately ending up, repeating requests "on several occasions to the U.S. Department of Justice and the Federal Bureau of Investigation," according to the Home Affairs Ministry's Thursday statement.  

The second source confirmed to CBS News that Washington did not meaningfully engage with the requests for help on the investigation and said it "would be useful to know" what Supermicro declared about its exports to fulfill orders by Megaspeed, whether those products were registered as being bound for Malaysia, and whether some or all of those products were actually "bound for somewhere else," such as China.

The Singapore home ministry said in its statement that six other individuals linked to Megaspeed, in addition to Alice Huang, are wanted for questioning, but none have been in the country since the government launched its investigation in February 2025. 

"One is a Singaporean citizen and the rest are foreigners," said the first person familiar with the case.

Singapore has charged five other people in a wider fraud conspiracy case related to the suspected transfer of Nvidia chips, including one Chinese man charged on Friday. The case was launched at the same time as the probe into Alice Huang and Megaspeed, the first source told CBS News, but it is separate.

"Singapore is committed to upholding our reputation as a trusted and reliable business hub. We will not allow companies or individuals to misuse Singapore's business environment to engage in fraud or dishonest practices," the home ministry said in its statement, adding that it would "conduct its own investigations independently, in accordance with our laws and based on the evidence available. We will cooperate with foreign authorities where appropriate, and take firm enforcement action wherever the evidence warrants it."

This story published first on CBS News at 12:16 p.m. on Nov. 13, 2026.

data.title: How Jensen Huang spent his last hours as Nvidia CEO
data.description:
‘I’m a Piece of Sh--’: Jensen Huang’s Last Hours as Nvidia CEO

Drake Bennett and Ian King
Thu, November 12, 2026 at 6:56 PM CST 6 min read
  • NVDA
    -2.49%

Learn more

(Bloomberg) -- At the end, Jensen Huang looked broken and shattered, his legendary energy depleted. After weeks spent denying the allegations of infidelity and fighting to remain in his job as Nvidia Corp.'s chief executive officer, his surrender late Wednesday night was unconditional. Huang's usual take-charge demeanor had evaporated, according to a person familiar with the situation, and he'd started using phrases like "whatever" and "I don't care."

Most Read from Bloomberg

  • Alice Huang, Suspected China Spy, Spent Years in Nvidia's Orbit

  • Nvidia Scandal Creates Risk for Entire AI Industry, Not Just CEO

  • Alleged Chinese Spy at Heart of Nvidia Scandal Is in Beijing

  • Mississippi Voters Pick Another Senator to Widen Democratic Win

  • Elon Musk Says It Would Be an Honor to Hire Nvidia's Huang

For the decades he spent building Nvidia into a multitrillion-dollar AI chip behemoth, Huang was famous for his attention to the tiniest of details, from chip architecture to the compensation packages of even the most junior employees at the company. Now, in the eyes of the people in the room, he had given up.

It was a stunningly quick fall for a billionaire and tech titan who two weeks ago was the face of artificial intelligence around the world. With his directness and vigor, he had charmed US President Donald Trump, shaped global tech policy and drawn adoring crowds on his papal-style international tours.

It's hard to imagine the current AI boom happening without Huang, his company and their chips, and it's hard to imagine what it will look like after his fall. As Harvey Jones, chair of the company's board of directors, wrote in an email to employees after Huang's ouster, "Jensen's contributions to Nvidia are profound. Nvidia is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world."

Huang couldn't be reached for comment.

When the news broke in late October that Huang had close ties with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy, it looked like he would prevail. The board of directors, dominated by longtime investors, business partners and friends of Huang's, was reluctant to act on the news stories, or even publicly comment on them.

Most of the news coverage tiptoed around the exact nature of the CEO's relationship with Alice Huang, the suspected spy. Huang denied to friends and colleagues that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He'd been denying it when questioned internally since late 2025. In one of his last interviews as CEO, Huang told Bloomberg News that his relationship with Alice Huang was typical of those with Chinese customers and executives. "It was all completely normal and not unusual," he said.

A turning point came last Friday, Nov. 6, when a Financial Times story cited US officials saying that the relationship had been a romantic one. Soon afterward, Nvidia general counsel Tim Teter went to Huang's house to confront him, and Huang confessed. At that point, most of the board still didn't want to take a public stance, but Teter, who is secretary of the board, told them they had to act. The next day, Saturday, the board announced that they would investigate the allegations. A prominent law firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, would lead the inquiry. On Sunday, Huang emailed the entire company, admitting to the affair, apologizing to his family and vowing to "cooperate fully" with the board's investigation.

As the scandal ballooned, there was evidence that it was, perhaps unsurprisingly, drawing Huang's attention away from his extensive duties at the company. As part of Nvidia's idiosyncratic org chart, Huang had around 60 executives at the company who reported to him, a small army by normal management standards. The whole company had to file emails with their top five priorities, which Huang used to check that everyone was working on what he considered most important. Normally he responded to them immediately at all hours of the day and night. In recent days the response times had grown longer.

On Wednesday, the New York Times reported that Huang was also having an extramarital relationship with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia's vice president of health care. This time, the board acted quickly. Directors assembled remotely on Wednesday, and the meeting lasted late into the night. In the end, Huang was given no choice but to resign, ending his association with the company completely.

The next morning, the board announced Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress would step in as interim CEO. She was quick to try and reassure rattled employees. "I believe deeply in this company and in its future," Kress wrote in an email reviewed by Bloomberg. "More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, staff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you."

She pledged to hold an all-hands meeting on Nov. 18. The following day, Nvidia is due to report results and disclose what Wall Steet analysts predict will be a near doubling of quarterly sales growth.

Now, the board confronts the difficult challenge of finding a replacement for Huang. Some executives considered likely to end up on the shortlist: Advanced Micro Devices Inc. CEO Lisa Su and Arm Holdings Plc CEO Rene Haas. It's hard to imagine anyone filling all his roles — technologist, executive, marketer, lobbyist, mascot — and the company never bothered to create a traditional succession plan. For better or worse, Nvidia will begin to look more like a regular company going forward, managed in a more regular way.

As for Huang himself, he won't be able to retreat from public life, even if he wants to. In the coming weeks he's expected to testify before Congress, where politicians will ask him about his relationship with Alice Huang and whether it might have put some of the secrets of Nvidia's state-of-the-art chips at risk. According to people who've spoken with him in recent days, Huang has already taken a penitent turn, castigating himself as a "piece of sh--." He claims not to care what happens to himself at this point. His main concern, he says, is his wife, and not "ruining the lives" of the multiple women now romantically linked to him in the public imagination.

data.title: Deadly building collapse brought Brooklyn neighbors together. Now they want answers.
data.description:
Emergency personnel work at the scene of a partial building collapse where, according to local reports, people are trapped in the Brooklyn borough of New York, on Wednesday, November 11.
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!
New York — 

Leonor Yupa dropped to her knees Thursday when a Spanish-language media reporter said her 22-year-old son was among eight people whose lives were claimed by the Brooklyn building collapse the day before.

“I want my son! I want my son!” the Ecuadorian mother cried in Spanish as family members tried to hold Yupa up and others who gathered at Bethesda Church of God in Christ assured her the reports were unconfirmed.

The agonizing cries of another woman who just lost her husband reverberated through the Brooklyn sanctuary across the street from the collapse. When the woman learned her husband’s body was pulled from the debris Thursday morning, she collapsed and wailed her husband’s name.

“Tomás! Tomasito!” she cried.

Family members gathered around the widow and formed a prayer circle.

Just outside the church, a nervous father also prayed. He was anxiously waiting to learn the fate of his son, a construction worker who has not been reachable since the collapse.

In the Flatbush neighborhood – home to a mix of immigrant communities – six adults and two children had died and over a dozen were injured after the three-story mixed-use building collapsed on Veterans Day, a day on which many families stayed home.

Locksmith captures immediate aftermath of the Brooklyn building collapse
0:50 • Source: CNN
Locksmith captures immediate aftermath of the Brooklyn building collapse
0:50

“I want to take a moment to remember those we have so senselessly lost,” Mayor Zohran Mamdani told reporters Thursday. “These were our friends and our neighbors, parents and children, young families building their lives in our city, and immigrants from Mexico, Colombia, Ecuador, Trinidad, and beyond.”

The day after the tragedy, residents and other bystanders crowded the sidewalk as construction equipment was used to removed debris and rubble from the site. Clothes still hung from a closet in an adjoining building where a wall came down during the collapse.

A construction worker embraces a child at the scene of the collapse on Wednesday.

A heavy rain pelted the intersection of Flatbush and Bedford avenues, a multicultural enclave that is the heart of New York City’s Caribbean diaspora. The names on signs of storefront churches and businesses – from bakeries, restaurants and beauty salons – reflect places like Jamaica, Haiti, Trinidad and Tobago, and more recently, newcomers from Mexico and Ecuador.

Among those killed Wednesday were three Colombian citizens, two Ecuadorian men and a 26-year-old Guatemalan man, officials from the countries announced.

In the aftermath of the collapse, local families, clergy and community groups gathered to support one another while demanding accountability for housing conditions and construction oversight in their predominantly Black and immigrant neighborhood.

‘Go in the church and pray, please’

On Wednesday night, Yupa and other relatives spent hours scouring hospitals throughout Brooklyn hoping to find her son, Gabriel Siguencia.

The family then visited the collapse site Thursday. Yupa shielded herself from heavy rain under the canopy of the church as a woman with a West Indian lilt alerted other bystanders nearby that she saw first responders pull a young child and a woman from the rubble.

Then came the news about Siguencia, who had arrived in New York from Ecuador only about a month ago and started working as a carpenter at the construction site adjacent to the building collapse about two weeks ago, according to uncles, cousins and family friends.

“He came to America looking for the same opportunities that people from all over the world come here for,” said family friend Javier Ortega, who drove Siguencia’s mother to the site from her home in Connecticut. “That’s why he was working there.”

Like many other families, Siguencia’s loved ones awaited news about him across the street from the collapse site. Some, like the husband of a six-month pregnant woman rescued from the rubble, rejoiced as they received word their loved one was safe.

First responders pull pregnant woman out of the rubble after Brooklyn building collapse
0:21 • Source: CNN
First responders pull pregnant woman out of the rubble after Brooklyn building collapse
0:21

As the downpour intensified Thursday over the neighborhood known as “Little Haiti,” a member of Bethesda Church of God in Christ invited Siguencia’s family inside the warm vestibule.

Yupa, weeping, sat on a folding chair as a Haitian church member served her cups of water. As Yupa sobbed, family members surrounded her and Ecuadoran consular officials made calls trying to track down information.

Soft murmurs of “Hallelujah, hallelujah” spilled out from the church filled with Haitian worshippers on the other side of the vestibule doors.

“We all have to look out for each other in this country,” said the woman who brought water to Yupa and the others. “It doesn’t matter where you come from.”

Another woman implored Yupa as she wept: “Go in the church and pray, please.”

Time ticked by with a heaviness before officials with the Ecuadoran consul walked Yupa and her friends and family members several blocks in the heavy rain to a nearby YMCA, where relatives of the dead and missing had been gathering.

The consul general of Ecuador, Gicela Andrade Valens, later told reporters outside that authorities had confirmed Siguencia’s death to his mother. Another Ecuadorian national, 26-year-old José Luis Caguana Cosquillo, was also killed.

“We express our deepest condolences to his family and loved ones, and we stand with them in profound solidarity in these moments of grief,” the consulate said.

Colombia’s consulate in New York said two Colombian children and one adult were killed in the collapse.

“The Consulate of Colombia in New York reiterates its most sincere condolences to the victims’ families and loved ones,” the consulate said.

‘Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood’

Pastor Alfred Justin Joseph’s church, the Bethesda Church of God in Christ, became an open sanctuary for the injured, the anxious and the grieving.

“They were standing in the street. I let them in,” Joseph said. “Thank God we have counselors in the church — people who do counseling for grief.”

Various groups have streamed through his church, including a dozen people in the first wave. While some have since been escorted to a local YMCA or hotels, the church remains an epicenter of consolation and support.

As she heard the wailing of the young woman who lost her spouse in the collapse, Flatbush resident Joy Kerr led a prayer circle to offer some comfort in a moment of devastation.

Kerr walked into the church and found the young woman crying hysterically after learning that her spouse, a construction worker, was killed when the building came down.

Kerr listened to the woman sobbing for about half an hour and said, “No, I can’t take this. I can’t sit back and just watch her and listen to her cry so hysterically.”

“In that moment, I knew she needed comfort,” she said.

She gathered with the woman who had lost her spouse and those around them, and they began to pray.

“This is devastating,” Kerr said. “Nothing like this has ever happened in this neighborhood, and we just need to come together and stay together as a community.”

A local teacher, Katie Stevens, shares emotional reaction to Brooklyn building collapse
1:15 • Source: CNN
A local teacher, Katie Stevens, shares emotional reaction to Brooklyn building collapse
1:15

And Katie Stevens, a teacher who lives about a block from the building, sobbed after she watched first responders load body bags into a van Thursday morning.

“I care for my neighbors so much,” Stevens told CNN. “I’m just so sad.”

James Williams, a bricklayer who has lived in the neighborhood for 35 years, stood across the street from the wreckage site Thursday and recalled watching the building’s walls cave in the day before.

One image reverberated in his mind: a woman climbing a now-exposed staircase as everything around her was crumbling.

“I don’t know if she got out alive or not,” he lamented. “To see that and not know what happened to her…I might have to go see a psychiatrist.”

Williams said he knows multiple families affected by the collapse. A friend told him she had been texting with relatives at the site when it collapsed but had not been able to locate them at any local hospitals.

As grief rippled through the neighborhood, nonprofits and agencies including the Red Cross, NYC Human Resources Administration and World Central Kitchen helped shaken families with emergency shelter, supplies and updates about missing people.

Neighbors call for accountability

Officials stand at the site on Thursday

As darkness fell over the collapse site Thursday night, amid thunderclaps and heavy rain, floodlights shone on a now-idle backhoe that had been excavating piles of debris, twisted metal and the pieces of what had been apartments into dumpsters.

Crews finished a marathon search through the rubble and determined there were no more survivors to be rescued, officials had said Thursday afternoon.

Under umbrellas, people hurried home after work, some stopping momentarily to look at the now-vacant space that had recently been home to many.

Across the street, a cluster of older women started gathering early for an evening service at Bethesda Church of God in Christ.

“This church happens to be a Haitian Creole speaking church, but the church is open to the entire community,” said Florence Saint-Jean, a psychologist who offers mental health and trauma services at the church.

“The people who live here are immigrants, and so when crisis happens, there’s only one language – love,” she said. “People are tired, they’re looking for food, they’re looking for shelter, and the church is always open and available.”

As neighbors hugged and comforted one another, one question created knots in their chests: How could this tragedy have happened?

The Department of Buildings has not yet determined the cause of the collapse, and an investigation is underway as new information emerges about the building’s history and construction process.

New York officials are looking into what caused the collapse of the building built in 1930, with Mamdani vowing to hold anyone responsible “fully accountable” and authorities inspecting about 100 locations throughout the city linked to the site.

The Brooklyn District Attorney’s Office is conducting its own investigation into whether laws were broken.

“We are working closely with the Department of Buildings and our law enforcement partners to determine whether any criminal conduct contributed to this tragedy,” district attorney Eric Gonzalez said in a statement Thursday.

As investigators try to determine factors in Wednesday’s deadly collapse of the three-story building in Brooklyn, they’ll be looking at both the condition of the collapsed building and activity at the construction site that neighbored it.

Cracks had been reported in the facade of the building as part of the permitting process for construction on the adjacent lot, which the collapse spilled into.

The building’s owner, Olufemi Falade, has a troubling history that reportedly landed him in jail for 12 days in 2006 for failing to repair hundreds of violations across multiple buildings.

The collapsed building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue currently has 98 open housing violations – ranging from unsafe electrical wiring and a lack of smoke detectors to bedbug infestations and a lack of adequate water supply for the building’s sprinkler system – according to records from the New York City Department of Housing Preservation and Development. CNN has reached out to Falade for comment.

Though building collapses are rare in the US, lower-income and immigrant neighborhoods often face higher risks of hazards and neglect.

Housing experts and advocates have pointed to systemic inequities that disproportionately impact working class immigrant communities, including old buildings, lax code enforcement and rapid construction.

Sumathy Kumar, executive director of New York State Tenant Bloc and Housing Justice for All, an organization that works to organize tenants, said the Brooklyn landlord has an extensive and troubling history with the city.

“We need better and faster tools to hold landlords accountable and to make sure that buildings are properly maintained and managed,” Kumar said.

Saint-Jean said there is a visible distinction between how development occurs in immigrant communities like Flatbush.

“What we’re most concerned about is, when things like his happen, that our voice (is) not being heard about development in the area,” she said.

CNN’s Ray Sanchez reported from New York and Dalia Faheid from Los Angeles. CNN’s Gloria Pazmino, Eduardo Cuevas, Brynn Gingras, Graham Hurley, Taylor Romine, John Miller and Holly Yan contributed to this report.
